title: Hurricane Maria
description:
B-roll package of family members of the Puerto Rico Air National Guard volunteering with the Emergency Family Assistance Center to build care pckages for service members affected by Hurricane Maria at Muniz Air National Guard Base, Puerto Riico, Oct. 10, 2017.
Hurricane Maria formed in the Atlantic Ocean and affected islands in the Caribbean Sea, including Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. U.S. Military assets supported FEMA as well as state and local authorities in rescue and relief efforts. (U.S. Air Force video by SrA Taylor Harrison)
keywords: ANG, relief efforts, Muniz Air National Guard Base, Hurricane Maria, NGB, Puerto Rico

transcript.text: Thank you so much for having us today.
My name is Kanda Louise Moore.
I go by Connie.
S-E-C-O-N-D-A-L-M-O-O-R-E.
In this capacity, I operate as the Emergency Family Assistance Center Director.
That's the E-FAC and that's to provide emergency assistance to the service members and the families
of the Puerto Rican International Guard.
And secondarily, we serve other service members and their families as well as we can.
And you know, later on I see that we might even get into outreach to some of the communities
as well.
Basically we have folks, stateside who are friends of the Guard, friends of different
organizations and units in the states that are preparing packages to us, things like comfort
items, comfort items are things like, you know, toothbrushes, toothpaste, deodorant, handy
wipes.
As you can see, we have quite a stash of water because water is a big need.
We also have food items as well and we will have some other larger items such as small
generators or small chainsaws because out in the community we have service members who
can't access the road from where they are at the moment but we'll go to them and make
sure that we get them lights for security, perhaps, you know, cut trees off their cars,
off their houses and in general improve their quality of life.
Well, the base commander is always the individual who the installation commander is always the
one who calls for an eFAC for an emergency family assistance center and they contacted
the National Guard Bureau.
Myself and several other people had volunteered.
I had the experience firsthand in a number of situations and so I was asked if I was
ready to come forward.
My back was already packed.
I didn't tell them it was because I was on vacation but I was quite ready to respond because
you know, it's all about making do with what you have and helping others as much as you
can.
So, NGB said, here's the letter of authority and my commander had approved it.
I'm actually the family program manager for the District of Columbia International Guard
stationed at Andrews Air Force Base, a job I've been doing for the last 17 years.
Our needs are varied and check with us before you start assembling goods and stuff and we
need for things to be marked correctly as gifts from friends of what organization.
We also need for them to placard it so that it comes to the 156th Puerto Rican International
Guard Emergency Family Assistance Center so that we can make distribution equitable to
all our service members.
We have about 1,200 service members who are going to be showing up for duty this coming
weekend and we want to make sure that we have those comfort items, those food items, things
that meet immediate needs into the hands of those that need them the most.
I have a staff in the EFAC that can handle legal, psychological, social, emotional, and so
I also have someone who can help them with FEMA claims, legal guidance and assistance and
a variety of social workers are available to me for those individuals who are just having
a very hard time dealing with life as we know it.
Things probably won't be getting back to normal for several months and there may be a continued
need here for our services as an EFAC.
An illustration is 9-11, the EFAC stood up over in Arlington, Virginia for a little better
than a month.
This is a natural disaster.
It may require three months, six months.
We have no way of knowing until all of the assessment is done.
We have combat photographers out there looking all over the island to identify the level of
this disaster.
We may very well have airmen, soldiers, Marines, Coast Guard, folks, military members who are
in those communities and cannot yet get out of them.
The scope of it could be quite large.
The biggest thing is if you're sending it here for distribution to military members you
need to identify it to come to the EFAC and we will certainly make sure that the goods
are distributed to service members and their families.
